title: The self in every being
hookLine: a saint pours the holy water he carried for Shiva into a thirsty donkey

cards: There's a story told about Eknath, a poet-saint of Maharashtra, about four hundred and fifty years ago.
He set out with pilgrims carrying water from the holy Ganga, a long walk south, to pour over Shiva at the great temple of Rameshwaram. A pilgrimage of months, and the water was precious.
On the road, in the heat, they came upon a donkey lying in the dust, dying of thirst. The others stepped around it. Eknath knelt, opened his pot, and poured the Ganga water into the donkey's mouth.
His companions were horrified. That water was for the Lord.

teach.b: Eknath's answer, as the story is usually told: the Lord just drank it. That's the Isha's sixth verse.
The one who sees all beings in the self, and the self in all beings, does not shrink away from anything.
The verb is vijugupsate: to recoil, to pull back in disgust. That's the flinch, named. And the cure isn't a rule; it's a way of seeing.
Hindus call the self within atman, and this verse says the same self looks out of every face. Pulling away from someone becomes like pulling away from your own hand.
Verse seven asks: for the one who sees oneness, ekatvam, what delusion is there, what sorrow? Verse eight praises the one who pervades all this: bright, bodiless, without wound, pure.
You met this in the Gita too, where the wise see the same in a scholar, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and a person everyone else cast out. Here's where it meets a day.
The everyday Hindu greeting, namaste, means I bow to you, and many teachers read it as the divine in me bowing to the divine in you.
At many temples, prasad goes to everyone in the line, the rich man and the man who slept outside. Seeing this way doesn't erase differences, and it doesn't mean staying near someone who hurts you.
It means the recoil loses its ground, because there's nobody there who isn't carrying the Lord.

how: Isha verses 6 and 7 are often quoted by Hindu teachers, especially in Vedanta, as the root of seeing one self in every being; many read the greeting namaste, 'I bow to you', in that light.

o: being alone, set apart from others
oneness, the same self in every being

games.q: verses six to eight — tap the pairs.
p: and the self in all beings
gave the Ganga water to a donkey

s: verse six says the cure for recoiling is to try harder to be nice
it's a way of seeing: all beings in the self, the self in all beings.
Eknath saved the Ganga water for the temple and walked past the donkey
he poured it into the donkey's mouth: the Lord, he said, just drank it.
verse seven asks what sorrow there is for one who sees oneness
it's phrased as a question: what delusion, what sorrow?

games.q: the man who sleeps outside the mandir is in the prasad line beside you. you feel yourself pull back. what does verse six say?
o: make sure you get yours first.
see the same self in him, and the pull-back loses its ground.
games.why: whoever sees all beings in the self, and the self in all beings, does not shrink away.

practice: Bring to mind someone mildly hard to be near, not the hardest person in your life, and notice the small pull back in your jaw or shoulders. Then fold your hands, the way you would for namaste.
If you pray, say silently: the same Lord is in you. If you don't, try: the same life breathing in me is breathing in you. See if the flinch softens a little; if it doesn't, that's fine, you looked.

wordCard.voice: Ekatva, oneness. For the one who sees oneness, what delusion is there, what sorrow? See all beings in the self, and the self in all beings, and stop shrinking back.

orig.note: Sanskrit: ekatva, oneness; verse seven: for the one who sees oneness, what delusion, what sorrow?

carryVoice: Your line: one self in every being. Eknath saw the Lord drink from a donkey's mouth. Until tomorrow.
